atoms.name: Assets & blob storage
atoms.oneLiner: Binary storage for images, imports and exports — behind a provider the platform core does not ship.
atoms.pattern: Port and adapter selected by configuration. `VirtoCommerce.Assets` owns the contract and the asset UI; a provider module supplies the backing store — `VirtoCommerce.AzureBlobAssets` for Azure Blob, `VirtoCommerce.FileSystemAssets` for local disk.
whenToUse: Anything binary: product images, attachments, generated documents, import and export files
Handing a caller a public URL for a stored blob, via `IBlobUrlResolver`
Claim-check for background jobs — store the file, pass its URL in the payload
avoid: The filesystem provider on more than one instance. Instances do not share a disk, so an upload lands on whichever node served the request
Storing binaries in the relational database
Serving large assets through the API instead of putting a CDN in front of blob storage
Assuming the abstraction exists in a bare platform — without the module there is no blob API at all

api.name: IBlobUrlResolver.GetAbsoluteUrl
api.file: (vc-module-assets — turns a blob key into a public URL)

atoms.note: There is no blob abstraction in `vc-platform` itself — verified by grep. `IBlobStorageProvider` lives in the Assets module, so a platform without it installed has no way to store a file beyond raw `System.IO`.
gotchas: Blob URLs are keys, not paths. Resolve to an absolute URL with `IBlobUrlResolver` before handing one to a client.
`IBlobStorageProvider` exposes sync and async pairs (`OpenRead` / `OpenReadAsync`). Prefer the async ones in request and job paths.
The filesystem provider is a development convenience. Scaling out without switching to blob storage produces missing-image bugs that affect only some requests.
Assets live outside the database, so they are outside its transactions and outside its backup.

atoms.name: Seq & log sinks
atoms.oneLiner: Sending structured logs somewhere you can query them, instead of reading console output.
atoms.pattern: Serilog sink added by configuration. The platform logs through `ILogger<T>` onto Serilog; a sink module such as `VirtoCommerce.SeqLog` forwards those events to a log server, where the structured properties become queryable fields.
whenToUse: Any environment where you cannot attach a debugger — which is every shared environment
Following one request or job across instances by correlating on a structured property
Turning "it failed yesterday for one customer" into a query rather than an archaeology exercise
avoid: Shipping personal data or secrets to a log server — it is a searchable index of whatever you send it
Debug level in production without a retention and volume plan
Relying on the console sink in a container nobody is watching
atoms.note: The module ships no interfaces of its own — it is wiring. You keep logging through `ILogger<T>` and the sink decides where events land; Application Insights is the other documented option.
gotchas: A sink is only as useful as your message templates. `LogInformation("Reindexed {StoreId}", id)` is queryable; an interpolated string is one opaque line and no sink can recover the property.
Sinks are configured, not coded — "logs are not arriving" is almost always the `Serilog` section rather than your code.
Log volume is a cost. The same sink that makes an incident tractable makes a chatty debug statement expensive.

atoms.name: Optional dependency
atoms.oneLiner: Declare a dependency you can live without, and the module still loads when it is absent.
atoms.pattern: Optional dependency, declared and resolved. `optional="true"` in the manifest takes the module out of the dependency solver and out of the installed-check; `IOptionalDependency<T>` is the runtime half, so code can ask whether the service is actually there.
whenToUse: A capability that enriches your module but is not required — the digital catalog runs without Pricing
Building a module set small enough to deploy on its own: an optional edge is an edge you can cut
Integrating with a module a customer may not have licensed or installed
Any `serviceCollection` consumer that must not throw when the provider module is missing
avoid: Marking a real requirement optional to make an install succeed — it will fail later, at a worse moment
Resolving the service in `Initialize` and caching it; ask through `IOptionalDependency<T>` at the point of use
Optional dependencies as a substitute for events. If you only need to be told something happened, handle the event instead

api.name: ModuleCatalog.SolveDependencies — optional edges are not added to the solver
ModuleBootstrapper — required-dependency errors and their cascade
IPricingEvaluatorService.EvaluateProductPricesAsync — the optional service in the snippet

gotchas: A **required** dependency that is missing is a hard gate: the module records `Module dependency {id} {version} is not installed` and every module depending on it is skipped with `Module skipped because its dependency has errors`. Optional edges are excluded from that cascade.

`IOptionalDependency<T>` resolves through `IServiceProvider.GetService<T>()` on every access, so `HasValue` reflects the host it is running in — the same code is correct in a full host and in a subset host.
Optional in the manifest and optional in code are two separate decisions. Declaring the edge optional without guarding the resolve gives you a null reference instead of a clear install error.
The dependency solver ignores optional edges entirely, so an optional dependency does **not** guarantee load order. Do not rely on the other module having initialised first.

atoms.name: Host composition
atoms.oneLiner: One image, several hosts: choose the module set per host, then choose the role per host in configuration.
atoms.pattern: Composition at deployment time, on two axes. **Which modules** a host contains comes from its package manifest; **which role** it plays comes from configuration. Neither needs a code change, and the second needs no separate image.
whenToUse: Isolating a workload so it cannot degrade another — background jobs away from checkout
Scaling one business capability on its own: a catalog-read host, sized for shopper traffic
Giving the back office and the storefront API separate failure domains
Cutting the surface of a host on purpose — fewer modules, fewer endpoints, smaller blast radius
avoid: Expecting a single module to become a service. The unit of deployment is a host with a module set, never one module
Splitting by role before Redis is in place — cache coherence, the SignalR backplane and the migration lock all depend on it
A module subset whose dependency graph does not close; the missing module takes its dependents down with it
More than one shape at once. Get all-in-one measured first, then split the axis your metrics point at

api.name: Startup lock — migrations run one host at a time
ModuleBootstrapper — discovery, probing and the resolved module set
vc-build install -PackageManifestPath — a different module set per image

snippet.code:
# Axis 1 — WHICH MODULES. Two manifests, two images, one source tree.
# vc-package.json         full host: everything the solution has
# vc-package.catalog.json catalog read path only

vc-build install -PackageManifestPath vc-package.catalog.json \
                 -ProbingPath ./app_data/modules

# Axis 2 — WHICH ROLE. Same image, same modules, configuration only.
#
#   storefront API   BackgroundJobs:Mode=Producer   ScalabilityMode=None            ARR off
#   back office      BackgroundJobs:Mode=Producer   ScalabilityMode=RedisBackplane  ARR on
#   job workers      BackgroundJobs:Mode=Worker     ScalabilityMode=None            ARR off
#
# As environment variables, so one image serves all three:
export BackgroundJobs__Mode=Worker
export PushNotifications__ScalabilityMode=None

gotchas: The dependency graph is the ceiling on a module subset. `VirtoCommerce.Orders` declares 11 dependencies — Cart, Catalog, Customer, Inventory, Notifications, Payment, Search, Shipping, Store, Assets, Core — so "orders on its own" is not a module set that exists.
Splitting by role changes nothing about the data: same modules, same database, same migrations. Splitting by module set is what changes the surface.
Every host that shares a database runs migrations at startup. That is safe only under the distributed lock, which needs Redis — see [[distributed-lock]].
A host without a module still shares the platform tables: settings, dynamic properties, permissions and module state are common ground.
Two images means two things to promote. The DevOps view has one image on purpose; a second one doubles the release surface.

atoms.name: Scalability
atoms.oneLiner: What is ready to scale out today, what will only ever scale up, and what has to be true before the second instance.
atoms.pattern: Stateless request path with shared state behind it. Every instance keeps a local memory cache and holds nothing else worth protecting, so capacity is a replica count; the state that cannot be replicated — one database writer, one index, one lock — is what you scale up instead. **Readiness is per level, not per platform**: some levels are ready out of the box, some are ready only vertically, and two are not ready at all.
whenToUse: **Ready to scale out, no work needed:** the request path (REST and XAPI) — it is stateless; the per-instance memory cache, once Redis carries invalidation; background jobs, via `Mode: Producer` and `Mode: Worker` hosts; a host per module subset; search, as an external cluster; assets, behind a cloud blob provider

**Every module can have its own database — one line, no code.** Each module registers its own `DbContext` and resolves its connection string by module id first: add `ConnectionStrings:VirtoCommerce.Pricing` and Pricing moves to its own server, migrations and all. The platform does this for identity itself with `Auth:ConnectionString`. It works because modules hold ids and copied values across a boundary, never foreign keys — so the split is a configuration change rather than a schema project. See [[module-database]] and [[cross-module-references]].

**Ready to scale up only:** the relational database — one writer, and read replicas where the provider allows; a single index rebuild; a single large import. More instances do not divide this work, a bigger machine does

**Not ready, and no configuration changes it:** a transaction spanning two module databases, and a single module as its own service. Both are design constraints rather than settings — see [[cross-module-references]] and [[host-composition]]
Before a launch, to decide the shape rather than discover it — the readiness list above is the checklist
When one workload is degrading another: the answer is usually another host, not a bigger one
avoid: Scaling up first. It buys headroom you pay for around the clock and hides the coupling that stopped you scaling out

Adding the second instance before the four prerequisites are met: Redis configured, a cloud blob provider instead of `FileSystemAssets`, a real search provider instead of Lucene, and the bearer-token certificate shared. Each of these works on one instance and fails on two
Scaling the database to fix catalog browse. The index is the read path; the database is not in it
Sizing every host the same. A 512 MB request host and a reindex worker want different machines
Quoting a scalability number without saying which level it applies to — the platform layer and your custom modules scale on different curves

api.name: VirtoCommerce:BackgroundJobs:Mode — Producer | Worker | Both, the horizontal split for jobs
SqlServer:CompatibilityLevel / ParameterTranslationMode — EF Core 10 query translation
DbContextRepositoryBase — command timeout inherited from the connection string
Startup lock — migrations serialised across instances

gotchas: `Connect Timeout` in the connection string becomes the **command** timeout: `DbContextRepositoryBase` reads it off the connection and calls `SetCommandTimeout` with it — since 3.1064 only when no command timeout was configured through the DbContext options, so a module that sets one keeps it. Raise it there and every query gets it, which is rarely what you want.

The migration lock is a scale-out dependency, not a nicety. Platform and module migrations run under the keyed startup lock (`VirtoCommerce.Platform.Startup`). Without Redis that lock is in-process, so two instances starting together can both migrate. With Redis, an instance that waits longer than `DistributedLock:WaitTime` (180 s) for another instance's migrations fails to start rather than migrating alongside it.

.NET reads its container limits and sizes the GC heap to them — in a container the GC treats the **container limit** as total physical memory, with a default heap hard limit of **75%** of it. Work that needs memory in bursts still does not fit: put a reindex or a bulk import on the jobs host and size that one for it.

**Server GC is the ASP.NET Core default, and it is not available on a single-core machine** — a 1-vCPU container silently runs Workstation GC. That is usually what you want there: Microsoft's guidance is that Server GC suits a machine the process dominates, while for **small containers and high-density hosting Workstation GC can be more performant**, and their own sample shows the working set dropping from ~500 MB to ~70 MB on the switch. Decide it per host role rather than once for the solution.

**DATAS is on by default from .NET 9**, which changes the shape of the question. It sizes the heap to the application rather than to the machine, starting at one heap and adding heaps under load — so the same image behaves similarly on a small container and a large one. Microsoft measures ~80% working-set improvement against a 2–3% throughput cost; if you are chasing that last 2%, `System.GC.DynamicAdaptationMode: 0` turns it off, and you own the consequences.

GC settings are read **once, at process start**, and are per process — so they belong in the image or the host's environment, never at machine level. `System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent` bounds the heap, and for a small process Microsoft suggests **raising** `System.GC.HighMemoryPercent` rather than lowering it, because a 1 GB process can run comfortably with less headroom than a 64 GB one.
A Redis **cluster** is not a drop-in replacement for a single instance — the platform uses operations whose semantics change across slots. Scale Redis up before you scale it out.
Sticky sessions belong on hosts serving the Commerce Manager UI and nowhere else. On stateless request hosts they defeat the load balancer for no benefit.

Two levels quietly refuse to scale out at all: `LuceneSearch` and `FileSystemAssets`. Both work on one instance and break on the second, which is why the provider swap is part of scaling rather than a later cleanup.

modules.name: Audit Log
modules.description: Provides extended audit features
modules.tagline: Provides extended audit features

notes.forAnalyst: A record of who changed what and when, for the changes a business must be able to explain.
notes.forArchitect: Three entities and nine migrations over one dependency, with five permissions. It is separate from the platform's change log because an audit trail has different retention and access rules from a developer-facing diff.
notes.forDeveloper: Two declared events. Volume is the design problem: decide what is audited and for how long before enabling it broadly, because everything is cheap to record and expensive to keep.
reachForItWhen: Compliance or a customer contract requires an audit trail
Disputes about who changed a price or an order must be settled
Access to sensitive data needs recording
doNotReachForItWhen: Debugging a data problem — the change log is closer to the code
You need operational telemetry: that is Application Insights
Retention is undecided: audit data grows without limit

keyFeatures: Subscribes to `GenericChangedEntryEvent<T>` and compares old/new snapshots.
Tracks **primitive properties** (string, int, enum, DateTime, …).
Tracks **primitive collections** (e.g. `IList<string> Tags`) via set equality.
Tracks **`IEntity` child collections** matched by `Id`.
Tracks **ValueObject child collections** matched by position.
Tracks **single `IEntity` / ValueObject child properties**.
Supports **deep nesting** — child records can carry their own child records (e.g. Contact → Organization → Address).
Each record stores operation type (`Added` / `Modified` / `Deleted`), changed fields with old/new values, and a tree of child records.
Domain events are processed **asynchronously** through a bounded `Channel<T>` and a background `IHostedService`, so event publishers are not blocked.
**`HttpLoggingMiddleware`** captures inbound request/response content for matching routes.
**`HttpTelemetryInitializer`** enriches outgoing `DependencyTelemetry` (Application Insights) with request/response content and headers.
Per-host / per-method / per-path rules with independent limits for request and response body length.
Settings are kept in a singleton in-memory cache, invalidated automatically when the management API mutates them. A pre-warm load starts at startup without holding it.

Cold-cache reads are bounded by a short timeout, so a slow database never blocks the request pipeline. The telemetry path bounds its wait on the thread that blocks, which holds even when the thread pool is saturated. A read that times out degrades to no HTTP logging for that item; the global redaction rules still apply to its URL.
Because the pre-warm is not awaited, the cache may still be cold when the first requests after a restart arrive, so that burst can meet the timeout and go unlogged, by design.

Tracked outgoing response bodies are captured as a bounded prefix, and the caller still receives the full body. The telemetry initializer runs before `HttpClient` reads the body, so it blocks the calling thread for at most `AuditLogOptions:HttpResponseCaptureTimeout` (default 1 s) waiting for that prefix; a body that does not arrive in time is logged as `<not captured>`. With `HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead` the caller can therefore get its headers up to that long later, and its first body bytes only once the whole prefix has arrived or the body has ended. Under body redaction rules the prefix is up to `MaxBodyLength` characters (1,048,576 by default, read as up to 4 MB of body), and with no response length set it is up to 1,048,576 characters the same way, so on a slow link a large body may exceed the timeout and go unlogged, and a response the caller reads as it arrives — NDJSON, a long poll — reaches it only in prefix-sized steps, and one that stays open sending less than a prefix reaches it only when it closes. Server-sent events (`text/event-stream`), gRPC and gRPC-Web (`application/grpc*`, requests too), `101 Switching Protocols` and `CONNECT` responses are not captured at all and are logged as `<not captured>`. `gzip`, `br` and `deflate` bodies are decoded for the log.

**Header names** (case-insensitive), or the inverse — an allow list that masks every header not explicitly permitted. Deny-by-default is the safer mode, because vendor header names are themselves injected from configuration. Allow-list mode with an empty list falls back to the built-in allow list rather than to the deny list, so opting out of the defaults cannot turn the strictest mode into the weakest one. There is consequently no configuration that means "mask every header": an empty list is read as "use the built-in one", and masking all of them would take listing them in `HeaderNames`.

**URI-valued headers** (`Location`, `Content-Location`, `Referer`, `Refresh`) have their query string redacted instead of being logged as an opaque string, and are masked whole when redaction is on but the query rules have been emptied — such a header is only in clear text because it was expected to be redacted, and both routes to that state ("Ignore default redaction", an explicitly empty `FormKeys`) are ones an operator takes to tighten things. With redaction off and no query rule left they are logged as they arrived; a setting's own `FormKeys` still apply even then, because an explicit per-setting rule is an explicit instruction. Without this a `302 Location: …?access_token=…` would carry the token past every other rule, while masking the header whole would throw away the redirect target.

**JsonPath** expressions for JSON bodies, including recursive descent (`$..password`). A plain `$..name` expression is matched **case-insensitively** — deliberately unlike JsonPath, because no literal list can enumerate every casing a field arrives under and the ones it misses are silent leaks. A different *name* still needs its own expression: `$..password` covers `Password` and `PASSWORD`, but neither `newPassword` nor `client_secret` against `clientSecret`. Expressions with a filter or an index (`$.records[*].fields`) are evaluated by Newtonsoft and keep its exact-match semantics.

**XPath** expressions for XML and SOAP bodies. Plain element names are matched by local name — inside predicates as well — so `//Credential[Identity='buyer']/SharedSecret` works for namespace-free cXML and for SOAP envelopes whose namespaces vary between endpoints. A namespace-sensitive name would make the expression select nothing, and unlike a malformed expression that failure is silent.

**Form and query keys** for `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` bodies, for the dependency URL, and for the inbound request URL — where OAuth tokens and blob SAS signatures appear. A form field that carries a whole document is decoded and run through the JsonPath/XPath rules too: the cXML punch-out return leg posts its response as one url-encoded field.

**Body kind** comes from the media type, but a declared type is a claim rather than proof, so the content overrides it wherever the content is unambiguous: JSON declared as `text/html` or as a form is still redacted as JSON, and a body declared as a form but not shaped like one is re-classified instead of passing through. A kind this module does not model still gets the key/value pass: every sensitive key it finds is masked, in any position, up to the next separator — and there whitespace counts as one, since that is how pairs arrive in an unstructured body. Only there: a query string and a declared form body are split on `&` alone, because a space inside a query-string value would otherwise end a mask early and publish the tail of the secret. `text/html` is never parsed as XML. A field value that fails to parse as a document is left alone when nothing a rule names appears in its text — which is what keeps error pages, pure diagnostics, readable — and masked when a rule name is in there, because the failed parse was then the only thing between that name's value and the log.

**Fail-safe**: when expressions apply to a body they cannot be applied to, a placeholder is logged instead of the raw body, and each cause has its own so the message names the real one — the body is unparsable, it holds content after the first document (which the parser itself accepted, such as NDJSON or a trailing comment), it is over the size limit, or an expression failed to evaluate. The last names the expression, so a typo is locatable rather than silently matching nothing.

Body length limits are enforced on the **redacted** copy, so a body long enough to be truncated is still redacted rather than dropped. A body over `MaxBodyLength` gets its own placeholder instead — see the option's row below.

Header names in `SecurityHeaderNames` (`Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Password`, …) are masked in **both** modes and cannot be un-masked by configuration — not by an allow list, not by `Enabled: false`, not by a setting's "Ignore default redaction".
Expressions come from the built-in defaults, from `AuditLogOptions:Redaction`, and from the individual HTTP dependency setting; the three are merged.

The **inbound request URL** is redacted by the telemetry initializer, not by the logging middleware: `HostingDiagnosticListener.EndRequest` assigns `RequestTelemetry.Url` unconditionally after the pipeline unwinds, so a value written from the middleware would be overwritten. Initializers run inside the `TrackRequest` call that follows that assignment.
REST endpoints under `api/audit-log` and `api/audit-log/http-dependency-setting/...`.
Module-scoped permissions: `AuditLog:access`, `AuditLog:read`, `AuditLog:create`, `AuditLog:update`, `AuditLog:delete`.

notes.forAnalyst: A way to tell other systems what happened in the store, through a message queue rather than a phone call: you subscribe a queue to the events you care about and the platform posts them there.
notes.forArchitect: The durable half of outbound integration, where WebHooks is the immediate half. It depends on nothing, keeps its own subscriptions and provider connections, and logs every connection attempt — four entities, one of which exists purely for that audit trail. Like WebHooks it subscribes to domain events **dynamically**, so any module's events become routable without it knowing about them. No admin UI: this is configured through its API.
notes.forDeveloper: Raise proper domain events in your own module and they become subscribable here for free — that is the whole contract. Choose this over WebHooks when delivery must survive the receiver being down, because a queue holds what an HTTP call drops. Subscriptions and provider connections are data, so a new integration is configuration rather than a release.

**Automatic domain event discovery** — scans all loaded assemblies at startup and exposes every `IEvent` implementation as a subscribable event

modules.name: Order Management (Business Rules)
modules.description: Consolidates order management business rules.
modules.tagline: Consolidates order management business rules.

notes.forAnalyst: The back-office workspace for handling orders — the queues, filters and actions a service agent uses all day.
notes.forArchitect: No storage and no schema: three dependencies and an optional fourth, five permissions, and a back office UI. It is a presentation layer over Orders, which is why it can be installed and removed without touching data.
notes.forDeveloper: Extend the workspace rather than the order document when the requirement is 'the agent needs to see X'. Nothing here is authoritative — a wrong value is Orders' to fix.
reachForItWhen: Agents work orders in bulk and need a purpose-built screen
The default order UI does not match how the team operates
You want to add actions without changing the order model
doNotReachForItWhen: The data model needs changing — that is Orders
A storefront needs order data: that is XOrder
You expect it to hold state: it holds none

keyFeatures: **Add products to an existing order.** `PUT api/order-management/add-items/{orderId}` appends new line items, evaluates prices via `VirtoCommerce.XCatalog` when available, and persists the order in a single round trip.

**Preserves unsaved UI edits.** After Add Product, previously-selected line-item statuses, edited quantities and prices, and any order-level edits are kept. The client reconciles the fresh server entity with the local state by diffing against the baseline so the user's in-flight work is not wiped.

**Correct optimistic concurrency after Add Product.** The client adopts the server-refreshed `rowVersion`/`modifiedDate` as part of the reconcile, so the next Save does not raise "The order has been modified by another user" (409).

**Clear validation of store references.** Add-items requests fail fast with an `InvalidOperationException` naming the missing store id when the order references a store that no longer exists, instead of bubbling a cryptic `NullReferenceException` from the catalog search pipeline.

**Resilient price evaluation.** Price lookup via `SearchProductQuery` is best-effort — if the pipeline is unavailable or fails for any reason, the new line item is still created (with Price = 0) and logged, rather than the whole request erroring out.
**Back Office toolbar buttons.** Registers **Add Product** and **Remove** toolbar actions on the Order Line Items blade.
**GraphQL schema scope `order-management`.** A scoped schema is exposed at the platform GraphQL endpoint for experience-API consumers.

modules.name: OTP Sign-In
modules.description: Enables customers to sign in to the storefront with a one-time code emailed to them, instead of a password.
modules.tagline: Enables customers to sign in to the storefront with a one-time code emailed to them, instead of a password.

notes.forAnalyst: Lets storefront customers sign in with a one-time code sent to their email instead of a password. It signs in existing customers only and does not create accounts.
notes.forArchitect: A custom grant type, `otp_email`, on the platform token endpoint, using the extension point added in 3.1075. Codes are generated and checked by the ASP.NET Core Identity email token provider, so the module stores nothing. It is switched on per store with `OtpSignIn.Enabled` (off by default) and depends on Customer, Notifications and Store.
notes.forDeveloper: The storefront calls `POST /api/otp/request` with `storeId` and `email`, then exchanges the code at `POST /connect/token` with `grant_type=otp_email`, `storeId`, `email` and `code`. Wrong codes count toward account lockout, and accounts with lockout disabled cannot use it. Any change to the user's security stamp, such as signing out in another session, invalidates codes already sent. The email is the `OtpSignInEmailNotification` notification.
reachForItWhen: Shoppers who forget passwords, or a storefront that does not want to manage them
Occasional B2B buyers who sign in rarely
doNotReachForItWhen: Self-registration by code: it signs in existing accounts only
A storefront with no rate limiting in front of it. Code requests are not rate-limited by the module, so limit `/api/otp/request` at the edge

modules.name: Passkeys
modules.description: Sign-in with passkeys (WebAuthn) for the Commerce Manager and the storefront, with creating, renaming and deleting passkeys.
modules.tagline: Sign-in with passkeys (WebAuthn) for the Commerce Manager and the storefront, with creating, renaming and deleting passkeys.

notes.forAnalyst: Lets people sign in with a passkey, using a fingerprint, face or device PIN, instead of a password, both in the back office and in the storefront. Users create, rename and delete their passkeys from their profile.
notes.forArchitect: WebAuthn on top of the platform's sign-in methods (3.1091): the module adds a `passkey` grant type on the token endpoint and registers passkeys as a sign-in method, so they appear next to passwords and external logins. The keys are stored in the platform's security database, which gained the passkey tables in 3.1091; the module has none of its own. It depends on xAPI and XFrontend because its storefront part is delivered as an XFrontend plugin; an Admin Shell plugin adds passkey sign-in to the new back office.
notes.forDeveloper: The passkey button and passkey creation appear only in browsers that support WebAuthn. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created on, so a passkey made for one host does not sign in on another. Each key shows its backup state (`DeviceOnly`, `BackedUp` or `NotBackedUp`), and a key without a name shows the authenticator's name from its AAGUID.
reachForItWhen: Removing passwords for back-office users, or offering a faster sign-in to returning customers
Phishing-resistant sign-in for privileged accounts
doNotReachForItWhen: Storefronts on several domains that expect one passkey to work on all of them
Storefronts that do not use XFrontend: the storefront part is delivered through it

keyFeatures: **Passwordless sign-in** — sign in with a passkey in the Commerce Manager and in the storefront
**Passkey management** — create passkeys from the user profile; rename and delete them through the platform's sign-in method API
**`passkey` grant type** — exchanges a WebAuthn assertion for a token on the token endpoint and on the platform's cookie sign-in endpoint; lockout and the platform's sign-in rules apply
**Readable key names** — a passkey without a name shows the authenticator's name, derived from its AAGUID
**Backup state** — each passkey shows whether it is `DeviceOnly`, `BackedUp` or `NotBackedUp`
**Storefront plugin** — adds the passkey sign-in button and passkey creation to the storefront through the XFrontend plugin system

**Admin Shell plugin** — adds "Sign in with a passkey" to the Admin Shell sign-in page and "Add a passkey" to its profile's sign-in methods, where passkeys are renamed and deleted (`AdminShellApp`, built into `plugins/admin-shell/`; `-p:SkipAdminShellPlugin=true` leaves it out)
**Browser detection** — the passkey button and passkey creation appear only when the browser supports WebAuthn
**Impersonation-safe** — passkeys cannot be created in an impersonated session

modules.name: Payment
modules.description: Provides management and integration of various payment methods.
modules.tagline: Provides management and integration of various payment methods.

notes.forAnalyst: Which ways a shopper may pay, per store — and the record of each attempt to collect the money. The module itself takes no payments; it is the list of methods, their settings and their status, with the actual gateway plugged in behind it.
notes.forArchitect: A port with its adapters shipped separately: NativePaymentMethods, AuthorizeNet, CyberSource, Datatrans and Skyflow are each their own module, so adding a gateway is an install rather than a change here. Two entities is all it owns — a method per store, and its translated name — because the transactions themselves belong to the order. Ten modules require it, so it is present on almost every host.
notes.forDeveloper: Implement a payment method against the module's abstraction and register it in code; the per-store configuration and its settings then appear in the back office without UI work. `PaymentMethodInstancingEvent` is the hook for adjusting a method as it is created — the place to inject solution-specific rates or restrictions.
reachForItWhen: A store needs a new way to pay, or an existing method configured differently
You are writing a gateway integration — implement the method, do not fork the module
Payment methods must vary by store, market or currency
doNotReachForItWhen: You need what was actually paid — that is the payment document on the order
You are reconciling money movements: captures, refunds and invoices live in Orders
The requirement is a wallet or stored card — that is the gateway's concern, and PCI scope with it

keyFeatures: **Extensible payment method registration** — Register custom payment methods via code using `IPaymentMethodsRegistrar.RegisterPaymentMethod<T>()`; payment methods are resolved through `AbstractTypeFactory` polymorphism
**Full payment lifecycle** — Abstract `PaymentMethod` base class supports Process, PostProcess, Void, Capture, and Refund operations with both synchronous (obsolete) and async APIs
**Per-store configuration** — Each payment method is persisted per store with settings for activation, priority, logo, deferred payment, partial payment availability, and localized display names
**Search and filtering** — Search payment methods by store, code, keyword, and active status; includes both persisted and transient (registered but not yet configured) methods in results
**Built-in manual payment method** — `DefaultManualPaymentMethod` provides an out-of-the-box payment method supporting capture and refund flows for manual/offline payment scenarios
**Localized display names** — Payment methods support localized names per language through the `PaymentMethodLocalizedName` entity
**Domain events** — Publishes `PaymentMethodChangeEvent` (before save), `PaymentMethodChangedEvent` (after save), and `PaymentMethodInstancingEvent` (before instantiation) for extensibility
**Export/Import** — Full platform export/import support for payment method configurations with batched processing
**Multi-database support** — Entity Framework Core migrations for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and MySQL
**Polymorphic JSON serialization** — Custom `PaymentMethodsJsonConverter` enables correct deserialization of payment method subtypes via the `TypeName` discriminator

notes.forAnalyst: Gives the back office a Reports entry that opens a Power BI sales dashboard and sales analysis report. The reports themselves are built and published in Power BI from a template the module provides.

A starting template for order and revenue reporting that a BI team will extend

modules.name: Pricing
modules.description: Robust pricing management functionality based on price list and dynamic evaluation
modules.tagline: Robust pricing management functionality based on price list and dynamic evaluation

notes.forAnalyst: What a product costs, and why: price lists, the assignments that decide which list applies to whom, and an evaluation step that picks the price for a given shopper, store and currency. A price is a decision made per request, not a number stored on the product.
notes.forArchitect: Small in schema — six entities against Catalog's 33 — and heavy in traffic, because evaluation runs on the read path. Its merged-price tables exist so the answer can be precomputed rather than derived per request. Two index builders project prices into the catalog index, which is the seam that makes price filtering possible and also the seam that goes stale after a bulk import: `Pricing.Search.EventBasedIndexation.Enable` is the switch to turn off before one.
notes.forDeveloper: Evaluate through `IPricingEvaluatorService` with a `PriceEvaluationContext` — never read a price row directly, or you will miss assignments, tiers and currency. `PriceChangedEvent` is what other modules subscribe to; the one that matters most is the handler that enqueues reindexing per changed SKU.
reachForItWhen: You need the price a specific shopper should see, in their store and currency
Pricing rules are the thing being modelled: lists, assignments, tiers, recommended prices
A bulk price import needs to be planned — this is where the indexation cost lands
doNotReachForItWhen: You want the price a customer actually paid — that is on the order line, copied at checkout
You are reading price rows to compute a price yourself: evaluation exists because assignment order is not obvious
You are importing thousands of price lists with events live — that fans out into one index job per SKU per list

keyFeatures: The system supports multiple **Pricelists**, i.e. the same product item may have different price in different price lists.
Each **Catalog** can have its own list of **Pricelists**.
Every **Pricelists** should have a unique Name-ID, and single currency.
Each **Pricelists** contains a list of product prices with single currency.
The system supports **Tier Pricing** and it is a way to encourage shoppers to buy larger quantities of a product by applying discounts based on the quantity ordered.
The system supports static discounts on products and allows the user to specify the discount on each item on the list.

In order to make the **Pricelists** active, it should be assigned to a specific **Catalog** in the system. The system allows the user to specify specific rules and conditions that can also be assigned to the **Pricelists**. These specific rules and conditions will influence the price calculation and define to which user categories or Organizations the pricelist will be displayed. This is a so-called **Dynamic Assignment**.
The system allows expanding the **Dynamic Assignment** tree and it completely depends on the organization business needs. Any condition or rule can be added without changing the Module logic.
The system allows assigning one **Pricelists** to several different **Catalogs**. The **Pricelists** is integrated into the **Catalog**.
The system allows specify the **Pricelists** priority and therefore display on **Storefront** the **Pricelists** with higher priority.

You are extending an existing query or mutation rather than adding an endpoint

You need a table: these modules own no schema, they compose other modules' services
Bulk writes: a mutation per row is slower than the owning module's import path

modules.name: Product Snapshot
modules.description:
The Product Snapshot module captures and stores product information at the moment an order is created.
  This ensures that customers and store operators always have access to the exact product details (prices, properties, images, descriptions)
  that were valid at the time of purchase, even if the product catalog is later modified or products are deleted.
modules.tagline:
The Product Snapshot module captures and stores product information at the moment an order is created.
  This ensures that customers and store operators always have access to the exact product details (prices, properties, images, descriptions)
  that were valid at the time of purchase, even if the product catalog is later modified or products are deleted.

notes.forAnalyst: A frozen copy of what a product looked like at a point in time — what the customer actually saw when they ordered.
notes.forArchitect: One entity and six migrations over three dependencies. It exists because Catalog is mutable and evidence must not be: this is the same instinct that makes an order line copy its price.
notes.forDeveloper: Two declared events mark snapshot creation. Snapshots grow without bound, so decide retention deliberately — nothing in the module will prune them for you.
reachForItWhen: Disputes need proof of what was displayed
Regulated products require a record of published claims
You must reconstruct a historical page
doNotReachForItWhen: Current product data is the question — read Catalog
You want change history of fields: that is the change log
Storage growth is unbudgeted

keyFeatures: **Automatic snapshot creation** — listens for the `OrderChangedEvent` and asynchronously creates product snapshots when a new order is placed.
**Full product data capture** — stores product info, assets, properties, and editorial reviews as a serialized JSON document.
**Configurable** — snapshot creation can be enabled or disabled through a platform setting.

**Catalog fallback** — products not covered by a snapshot are loaded by xOrder's `OrderProductResolver.LoadProductsAsync` from the live catalog. The fallback is provided by xOrder, not by this module.
**Granular permissions** — access, create, read, update, and delete operations are controlled by dedicated permissions.

**Extendable Product Snapshot Page** - the module provides extension points (productSnapshotDetails metaform and widget-container) on the Product Snapshot details page to display custom information related to the snapshot, such as links to related orders or custom product attributes.
**REST API** — retrieve a product snapshot via `GET /api/product-snapshots/order/{orderId}/product/{productId}`.

**GraphQL / Experience API integration** — the `LoadorderProductSnapshotMiddleware` transparently injects snapshots into the `ExternalOrderProducts` pipeline, so X-Order consumers receive snapshot data without additional queries.
**Multi-database support** — SQL Server, MySQL, and PostgreSQL are supported out of the box.

**Async snapshot creation (Soon)** — snapshot generation runs in the background to avoid impacting order processing performance. If snapshot creation fails, it is logged but does not block the order from being created.

modules.name: Rating and Reviews
modules.description: Enables customers to share their feedback on products and vendors after making a purchase, helping others make informed decisions.
modules.tagline: Enables customers to share their feedback on products and vendors after making a purchase, helping others make informed decisions.

notes.forAnalyst: Ratings and written reviews on products, with moderation before they appear.
notes.forArchitect: Ten required dependencies — surprising for a review module, and the reason is that a review touches catalog, customer, order (verified purchase) and notifications. Four entities, ten settings for moderation and rating rules, two GraphQL builders for the storefront.
notes.forDeveloper: Three declared events cover submission and moderation, which is where notification and recalculation hang. Aggregate ratings are derived — decide deliberately whether they are computed live or projected into the index.
reachForItWhen: Social proof is a requirement and moderation is not optional
Reviews must be tied to verified purchases
Ratings should be filterable on the storefront
doNotReachForItWhen: You only need a star field on a product — that is a catalog property
Reviews live in an external service that owns moderation
The host must stay small: ten dependencies say otherwise

keyFeatures: **Review lifecycle management** — create, update, moderate (approve/reject/reset), and delete reviews through the Admin Portal or REST API.
**Rich review content** — title, body, numeric rating, and up to N attached images per review (configurable).

**Rating aggregation** — pluggable rating calculators with two built-in strategies: `Average` and [Wilson lower bound](https://www.evanmiller.org/how-not-to-sort-by-average-rating.html). Ratings are computed per entity and per store.
**Multi-store and store-agnostic support** — each store maintains its own ratings and can be configured independently; non-store-scoped reviews are also supported.
**Flexible entity model** — reviews are keyed by `EntityId` + `EntityType`, so additional object types (vendor, order, custom objects) can be registered without modifying the module's source code.
**Anonymous vs. authenticated reviews** — per-store toggle to allow or require a signed-in user.
**"Purchase-verified" reviews** — optional store-level rule restricting reviews to customers who have previously ordered the product.

**Email review reminders** — recurring Hangfire job that emails buyers after their order reaches a configured status (e.g. `Completed`), prompting them to leave feedback. Reminder cadence, eligibility window, and the maximum number of reminders per customer are all configurable.
**GraphQL (xAPI) integration** — storefront-facing GraphQL schema for querying reviews, checking whether the current user can leave feedback, and submitting new reviews.
**Image uploads** — integrates with `VirtoCommerce.FileExperienceApi` / Assets for a dedicated `review-images` scope.

**Event-driven integrations** — publishes `CustomerReviewChangeEvent`, `CustomerReviewChangedEvent`, and `ReviewStatusChangedEvent` so other modules can react to moderation changes and rating recalculations.
**Multi-database support** — ships with EF Core providers for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and MySQL.
**Permissions-aware Admin UI** — fine-grained permissions for reading reviews, updating, deleting, reading ratings, and triggering rating recalculation.

modules.name: Search Core
modules.description: Defines Core Abstractions for indexed search functionality above different search providers, like: Elasticsearch, Azure Search, etc.
modules.tagline: Defines Core Abstractions for indexed search functionality above different search providers, like: Elasticsearch, Azure Search, etc.

notes.forAnalyst: The engine room behind every product list, filter and search box. It holds no business data of its own — it describes how other modules' data is turned into searchable documents, and keeps those documents in step with the database.
notes.forArchitect: The clearest port-and-adapter in the platform: **no database, no entities, no migrations, and no module dependencies**. Providers — Elasticsearch, Azure Search, OpenSearch, Algolia, Lucene — plug in behind it, and twelve document builders are contributed by the modules that own the data. That inversion is why Catalog, Customer, Orders and Pricing all list Search as a dependency and none of them knows which engine is running. Indexing is a background job, so an index host and a request host can be different machines.
notes.forDeveloper: Contribute an `IIndexDocumentBuilder` for your own entity rather than writing to the index directly, and let the changes provider tell the job what moved. `VirtoCommerce.Search.IndexingJobs.CronExpression` and `.Enable` control the schedule; `search:index:rebuild` is the permission behind a full reindex. Partial document update exists for the case where one field changed and the whole document need not be rebuilt.
reachForItWhen: Anything must be searchable, filterable or facetable at storefront scale
You are adding your own entity to the index — write a document builder, not an index writer
A provider needs swapping, or a second index has to be built alongside the live one
doNotReachForItWhen: You need a transactional read of the current row — the index is eventually consistent, on purpose
You are looking for the data itself: this module stores none of it
A single record must be correct the instant it is written — read the owning module, not the index

keyFeatures: **Pluggable provider model**: swap search engines without changing the rest of the platform.
**Multi-document support**: index and search multiple document types in a unified way.
**Per-document provider & scope routing**: select provider/scope per document type via configuration.
**Indexing orchestration**: supports full rebuild and incremental “changes” indexation.
**Blue-green indexation support**: supports backup indices and index swap for providers that implement it.
**Scheduled background jobs**: recurring indexation via Hangfire, controllable by platform settings.
**Search phrase parsing**: query/phrase parsing infrastructure (ANTLR-based) for consistent request building.
**Admin integration**: API endpoints, permissions, and back office UI assets/localization for managing indexing.

modules.name: SEO
modules.description: Infrastructure for managing SEO metadata across the platform
modules.tagline: Infrastructure for managing SEO metadata across the platform

notes.forAnalyst: The addresses your storefront exposes to the world: friendly URLs for products, categories and pages, redirects when something moves, and a record of links that now lead nowhere.
notes.forArchitect: It depends on nothing and resolves permalinks through a scoring pipeline, which is what lets one slug belong to different objects in different stores and languages without ambiguity. The interesting seam is that it both **raises and handles** `SeoInfoNotFoundEvent`: a miss becomes an event other modules can answer, which is how a custom resolver joins the pipeline instead of replacing it. Broken-link detection is a switch, not an assumption.
notes.forDeveloper: Subscribe to `SeoInfoNotFoundEvent` to resolve a slug your own module owns; do not fork the resolver. `Seo.Enabled` and `Seo.BrokenLinkDetection.Enabled` gate the module's work, so a headless or API-only deployment can turn it off entirely. Redirect rules are data, so marketing can move a URL without a release.
reachForItWhen: A URL has to be friendly, stable, or moved without breaking inbound links
Your module owns objects that need addressable slugs per store and language
You need to know which links are broken before a customer finds out
doNotReachForItWhen: The page content is the question — that is Content
You are building an API-only solution with no crawlable surface: turn it off instead
You want analytics on traffic: this module records broken links, not visits

keyFeatures: **SEO Metadata Resolution** — Resolves SEO records (slugs, page titles, meta descriptions, keywords) per entity, store, language, and organization using a composite resolver that aggregates multiple `ISeoResolver` implementations.

**Best-Match Scoring Pipeline** — A 6-stage pipeline (Original, Filtered, Scored, FilteredScore, Ordered, Final) selects the most relevant SEO entry when multiple candidates match a permalink, with configurable object type priorities.
**Redirect Rules** — Static or regex-based URL rewrite rules with priority ordering and capture group substitution (`$1`, `$2`, etc.), validated via FluentValidation.

**Broken Link Detection** — Event-driven tracking of unresolved permalinks. When no SEO info is found, a `SeoInfoNotFoundEvent` triggers a Hangfire background job that records or updates the broken link with hit count and timestamp.
**SEO Duplicates Detection** — Extensible `ISeoDuplicatesDetector` interface for identifying conflicting SEO entries within an object's relationships (default implementation is a no-op).

**Explain / Debug Tool** — REST API endpoint and Admin UI widget that traces the full permalink resolution pipeline stage by stage for diagnostics, including the SEO records a resolver rejected and why.
**Export / Import** — Streaming JSON-based export and import of redirect rules and broken links with batch processing (100 items per batch) and progress reporting.
**Multi-Database Support** — EF Core providers for SQL Server, MySQL, and PostgreSQL with version-controlled migrations.

An incident needs traces or metrics that survive a restart
The hosting platform already collects this format

modules.description: Add shipping methods management
modules.tagline: Add shipping methods management

notes.forAnalyst: How goods reach the buyer: the shipping methods a store offers, their rates, and — for buy-online, pick-up-in-store — the physical locations a shopper can collect from.
notes.forArchitect: The same port-and-adapter shape as Payment, with ShipStation as the external adapter, plus one thing Payment does not have: pickup locations are searchable, which is why Search is a required dependency and why `Shipping.Bopis.Search.EventBasedIndexation.Enabled` exists. notes.forDeveloper: Register a shipping method in code and let the store configure it; each method carries its own settings. Pickup locations have their own change events and their own indexation date setting, so a bulk import of locations needs the same treatment as any other indexed entity. Google Maps keys for BOPIS are settings.
reachForItWhen: A store needs new shipping options, or rates have to differ by store
Click-and-collect is in scope — pickup locations and their fulfillment relations live here
You are integrating a carrier or rate service
doNotReachForItWhen: You need what was shipped — that is a shipment document on the order
Stock at a location is the question: that is Inventory's fulfillment centre
You want tracking history: the carrier owns it, and the order records the reference

Public REST API to work with shipping methods, pickup locations and indexed search.

modules.name: Shopping Cart
modules.description: Shopping cart / checkout functionality
modules.tagline: Shopping cart / checkout functionality

notes.forAnalyst: The basket a shopper is filling, including named wish lists, and what it totals before checkout — line items, discounts, coupons, shipments, payments and taxes as they stand right now. Nothing here is a record of a sale; it is the state of an intention.
notes.forArchitect: A high-churn store with no back-office UI: it is written on almost every storefront interaction, and it needs seven modules to be present — Assets, Core, Customer, Notifications, Payment, Shipping, Store — which makes it a poor candidate for a small host. notes.forDeveloper: Two declared events, `CartChangeEvent` before the save and `CartChangedEvent` after it, are how you hook cart behaviour without forking the module — validation and totals recalculation both ride on them. `api/carts` carries 24 actions; the storefront path is xCart, not this REST surface.

Checkout has to recalculate totals, taxes or shipping before an order exists
doNotReachForItWhen: The sale has happened — an order is a separate document in Orders, with its own copy of the prices
You want cart history or analytics: carts are pruned on a schedule and are not an archive
You are on a storefront: talk to xCart, which is built for one round trip per page

Compliance scope has to be reduced deliberately

The data lives across modules that own their own schemas: joins here couple you to them

modules.name: Store
modules.description: Multi store management with individual store settings
modules.tagline: Multi store management with individual store settings

notes.forAnalyst: Each storefront as a configurable thing: its languages, currencies, the fulfillment centres it ships from, its email verification and anonymous-shopping rules, and which other stores it trusts. One installation can run many brands or markets from here.
notes.forArchitect: The tenancy seam of a Virto solution. Almost every commerce module takes a `storeId` and resolves behaviour through this module, which is why Cart, Catalog, Orders, Content and Marketing all list it as a required dependency — and why it, in turn, depends on almost nothing (Core, Notifications, Seo). Trusted groups make cross-store data sharing explicit rather than implied.

Note it exposes a single permission, `store:read` — store configuration is read widely and written rarely, so authorisation for writes lives with the platform's module-management permissions.

Data has to be shared between stores deliberately, through trusted groups

modules.name: Webhooks
modules.description: Manage user defined webhooks
modules.tagline: Manage user defined webhooks

notes.forAnalyst: Lets the business subscribe an external system to things that happen in the store — an order placed, a price changed — without a developer writing an integration for each one. Someone configures the endpoint and the fields to send in the back office, and every delivery attempt is auditable afterwards.
notes.forArchitect: The platform's only built-in outbound integration edge. It turns in-process domain events into HTTP POSTs, which means it is the boundary where a Virto event stops being transactional: delivery is a background job with retries, not part of the writing transaction. It declares no module dependencies, so it can be installed on any host — but it needs a background-jobs worker to deliver anything, and it owns four tables of its own.
notes.forDeveloper: You rarely code against it. Raise a proper domain event in your module and it becomes subscribable automatically, because the module resolves DomainEvent types from every loaded assembly at runtime. The two knobs that change behaviour are settings, not code: Webhooks.General.SendRetryCount and Webhooks.General.LatestErrorCount.
reachForItWhen: An external system needs to react to store changes and you do not want it polling your API
Integration middleware wants a change stream rather than a nightly diff
A partner asked for callbacks and you need the delivery attempts on record
doNotReachForItWhen: The reaction belongs inside the platform — that is a domain event handler, in-process and transactional
You need guaranteed, ordered delivery: this is retried HTTP with exponential backoff, not a broker. Reach for EventBus and a real queue
The payload would carry data the receiving endpoint should not see — field selection is per webhook and easy to over-share
The events come from a bulk import: suppress events or turn event-based indexation off first, or one import fans out into thousands of callbacks

keyFeatures: **Automatic event discovery** — resolves all `DomainEvent` types from the platform and installed modules at runtime
**Selective payload composition** — choose specific entity properties to include in the notification body, with access to previous values for change tracking
**Multiple authentication schemes** — None, HTTP Basic, Bearer Token, and Custom Header
**Resilient delivery** — configurable retry policy with exponential backoff powered by Polly (default: 3 retries at 1, 2, 4 minute intervals)
**Execution audit log (Feed)** — records request/response headers, body, HTTP status, error messages, and attempt counts for every webhook invocation
**Background processing** — notifications are dispatched asynchronously via Hangfire with a 5-second debounce delay and processed in batches of 20
**Permission-based access control** — granular permissions for read, update, delete, and feed access
**Multi-database support** — SQL Server, MySQL, and PostgreSQL via dedicated EF Core provider assemblies
